fixes.d: Witnesses told investigators in 1996–97 of abuse parties and unsolved murders involving Marc Dutroux, Michel Nihoul and prominent people. Prosecutors ultimately dismissed the statements, and investigators were criticised for leading a key witness; an officer charged in 1997 with falsifying her statements was cleared in 1999. In 1999 the Guardian reported renewed cover-up claims, and that the parliamentary inquiry's chair said his findings had been muzzled. The claims of an elite network remain unproven; a 1999 book by three journalists argued the witnesses were more credible than portrayed.

cite: Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse, 'Allegations of child sexual abuse linked to Westminster', investigation report, conclusions (K.1), 25 February 2020

fixes.d: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse examined how Parliament, political parties, the police, prosecutors and the honours system dealt with allegations of child sexual abuse involving people connected to Westminster, and reported on 25 February 2020. It found "no evidence to suggest an organised network of abusers in Westminster". It did find "overt and direct deference by police towards powerful people", that the diplomat Sir Peter Hayman "was the beneficiary of preferential, differential and unduly deferential treatment", that party whips' offices were "concerned above all to protect the image of their party" though there was no evidence they deliberately suppressed specific information, that the former Liberal leader David Steel "yielded to considerations of political expediency" over Cyril Smith, and that the honours system in some instances "prioritised reputation and discretion with little or no regard for victims".
fixes.cover: The inquiry concluded that "deference to class and power was the overriding motive" for decisions in the Montagu and Hayman cases, and that the police showed "a patronising attitude" towards a working-class victim in the Montagu case.
